title: Orbit Foundry: keeping an AI-coded incremental's simulation separate from its browser shell
author: kimchistan_game
selftext:
I'm developing Orbit Foundry, a space incremental where machines affect neighboring production and timed reactor pulses add an active bonus. The game's code is generated with Codex CLI, and AI also assisted with some translations.



One concrete part of the implementation is the boundary between the game and its browser wrapper. Gameplay, progression and save validation live in Lua with LÖVE; the browser shell handles loading the WebAssembly runtime, storage, imports, downloads and fullscreen. Neighboring production bonuses are non-recursive, so the placement preview can compare an arrangement without creating a feedback loop between machines.



The project has pure Lua regression tests for economy, progression and saves, alongside separate browser/UI checks. That separates questions like whether a save survives a round trip from whether a player can actually understand and use the placement controls. A passing calculation test doesn't settle the second question.



For others building incrementals with AI, which edge cases do you prioritize before adding another progression system: offline catch-up, automation spending, save migration, or something else? I'd be interested in concrete failure cases worth testing.



The free 2D demo is playable in a desktop browser, with no download or account: [https://kimchistan.itch.io/orbit-foundry](https://kimchistan.itch.io/orbit-foundry)



That demo is the LÖVE 2D build; a separate Godot 3D version is in development.
